source_text: Dixi, quod erat primum, scientiam boni non esse uirtutem, deinde, quid sit uirtus et in quo sit: sequitur ut id quoque ipsum, quid sit bonum et malum, nescisse philosophos breuiter ostendam, quia paene declaratum est in libro tertio, cum de summo bono disputarem. qui autem quid esset summum nescierunt, et in ceteris bonis malisue, quae summa non sunt, errauerint necesse est: quae non potest uero iudicio examinare qui fontem ipsum non tenet unde illa descendunt. fons autem bonorum deus est, malorum uero ille scilicet diuini nominis semper inimicus, de quo saepe diximus: ab his duobus principiis bona malaque oriuntur. quae ueniunt a deo, hanc habent rationem, ut inmortalitatem parent, quod est summum bonum: quae autem ab illo altero, id habent officium, ut a caelestibus auocatum terrenisque demersum ad poenam interficiant sempiternam, quod est summum malum. num igitur dubium est quin illi omnes quid esset bonum et malum ignoraueriut, qui nec deum nec aduersarium dei scierunt? itaque finem bonorum ad corpus et ad hanc uitam breuem retulerunt, quam scilicet solui et occidere necesse est, non sunt progressi ulterius, sed omnia eorum praecepta et omnia quae inducunt bona, terrae inhaerent et humi iacent, quoniam simul cum corpore, quod est terra, moriuntur. pertinent enim non ad uitam homini conparandam, sed ad quaerendas uel augendas opes honores gloriam potentiam: quae sunt uniuersa mortalia, tam scilicet quam ille qui ut ea sibi contingerent laborauit. hinc est illud: uirtus, quaerendae finem rei scire modumque. praecipiunt enim quibus modis et quibus artibus res familiaris quaerenda sit, quia uident male quaeri solere. sed huiusmodi uirtus non est proposita sapienti: nec enim uirtus est opes quaerere, quarum neque inuentio neque possessio in nostra potestate est. itaque et quaesitu et obtentu faciliores sunt malis quam bonis. non potest ergo uirtus esse in iis rebus quaerendis in quarum contemptu uis ac ratio uirtutis apparet, nec ad ea ipsa transfugiet quae magno et excelso animo calcare ac proterere gestit, neque fas est animam caelestibus intentam bonis, ut haec fragilia sibi conparet, ab inmortalibus suis opibus auocari, sed potissimum in iis rebus conparandis uirtutis ratio consistit quas nobis nec homo ullus nec mors ipsa possit auferre.
pass_a_gloss: I said, which was first, that knowledge of good is not virtue, then, what virtue is and in what it is: it follows that I must also briefly show that philosophers were ignorant of what good and evil are, because it was almost declared in the third book, when I was disputing about the highest good. those who did not know what the highest good was, and in other goods and evils, which are not the highest, necessarily erred: because one who does not hold the source itself from which those things come cannot truly examine them by judgment. the source of goods is God, but of evils, that one, namely, the enemy of the divine name, about whom we have often spoken: goods and evils arise from these two principles. those things which come from God have this reason, that they bring about immortality, which is the highest good: those things which come from that other one have this function, that they kill and destroy, having been called away from heavenly things and immersed in earthly things, to eternal punishment, which is the highest evil. is it therefore doubtful that all those who did not know God or the adversary of God were ignorant of what good and evil are? and so they referred the end of goods to the body and to this brief life, which must be dissolved and killed, they did not progress further, but all their precepts and all the goods they introduce are attached to the earth and lie on the ground, because they die together with the body, which is earth. for they pertain not to the life of man to be compared, but to seeking or increasing wealth, honors, glory, power: which are all mortal, just as the one who labored so that these things might happen to him. from this comes that saying: virtue is to know the end and measure of a thing. for they teach by what means and arts family wealth is to be sought, because they see that it is usually sought in a bad way. but such virtue is not proposed to the wise: for virtue is not to seek wealth, the discovery and possession of which are not in our power. and so they are easier to seek and obtain in evils than in goods. therefore, virtue cannot be in those things which are sought, in whose contempt the power and reason of virtue appear, nor will it flee to those things which it desires to trample and despise with a great and lofty mind, nor is it right that the soul, intent on heavenly goods, should be called away from its immortal goods to compare these fragile things to itself, but rather the reason of virtue consists in those things which no man or death itself can take away from us.
pass_b_english: I stated first that knowledge of the good is not virtue, then what virtue is and where it resides; it follows that I must also briefly demonstrate that the philosophers were ignorant of what good and evil are, since this was nearly established in the third book when I was disputing about the highest good. Those who did not know what the highest good was necessarily erred concerning other goods and evils, which are not the highest, because one who does not grasp the very source from which these things descend cannot truly judge them. The source of goods is God; the source of evils is that one, namely the enemy of the divine name, of whom we have often spoken. Goods and evils arise from these two principles. Those things that come from God have this character: they bring about immortality, which is the highest good. Those things that come from that other one have this function: they kill and destroy, having been called away from heavenly things and immersed in earthly things, to eternal punishment, which is the highest evil. Is it therefore doubtful that all those who knew neither God nor the adversary of God were ignorant of what good and evil are? Consequently, they referred the end of goods to the body and to this brief life, which must be dissolved and killed; they did not progress further, but all their precepts and all the goods they introduce cling to the earth and lie on the ground, because they die together with the body, which is earth. For they pertain not to procuring life for man, but to seeking or increasing wealth, honors, glory, and power — all of which are mortal, just like the man who labored that these things might befall him. Hence comes that saying: virtue is to know the end and measure of a thing. For they teach by what means and arts family wealth is to be sought, because they see that it is usually sought badly. But such virtue is not proposed to the wise; for virtue is not to seek wealth, the discovery and possession of which are not in our power. Thus wealth is easier to seek and obtain through evil than through good. Therefore virtue cannot reside in those things which are sought, in whose contempt the power and reason of virtue appear; nor will it flee to those things which it desires to trample and despise with a great and lofty mind; nor is it right that the soul, intent on heavenly goods, should be called away from its immortal goods to compare these fragile things to itself. Rather, the reason of virtue consists in those things which neither any man nor death itself can take away from us.
